title: Make the visual serve the selling idea.
dek: In Chapter 7 of Tested Advertising Methods, John Caples explains when pictures strengthen an advertisement and when they merely decorate it.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A picture earns its place when it makes the promise easier to understand, believe, or want. Decoration is not persuasion.

canon.heading: Make the picture carry part of the sale.
canon.standfirst: Read the bounded opening of Chapter 7, "The Use of Pictures," from John Caples's Tested Advertising Methods on printed pages 71-80. Study how visual treatment can clarify and intensify a selling idea, then stop at printed page 80.
canon.readerIntro: Read this section as a test of function. Mark where a picture demonstrates, dramatises, proves, or focuses the promise, and where it risks becoming decoration. Then audit one advertisement: name the selling idea, the visual job, and the evidence that the image helps the reader understand or desire the offer. Stop at printed page 80.

blocks.label: 01 / Start with the selling idea
paragraphs: Identify the promise before judging the picture.
Notice whether the visual makes that promise clearer, more vivid, or more believable.

blocks.label: 02 / Separate demonstration from decoration
paragraphs: A useful image shows the product, result, mechanism, or situation in a way words alone cannot.
Mark the point where visual interest stops serving the reader's decision.

blocks.label: 03 / Run one visual-selling audit
paragraphs: Choose one advertisement and write its selling idea in one sentence.
Then name the image's job and one change that would make its contribution to the sale unmistakable.

closeReading: What makes a picture contribute to the selling idea rather than merely attract attention?
Where does Caples distinguish visual evidence from visual decoration?
Which kind of offer benefits most from demonstration, and why?
Choose one advertisement: what is the selling idea, what job does the picture perform, and what would improve that job?

principle.heading: Give the picture a job in the sale.
principle.body: Visual treatment is strongest when it makes the offer easier to see, understand, believe, or desire. The image should serve the promise, not compete with it.
principle.example: A meal-kit ad should show the finished dinner and the ease of preparing it if those are the reasons to buy, not an unrelated lifestyle scene that earns attention but leaves the offer vague.
principle.practice: Choose one advertisement. Write its selling idea, the visual job required to support it, and one change that would make the image more useful to the reader's decision.

output.heading: Make attention end in understanding.
output.body: The best picture is not simply memorable. It helps the reader grasp why the offer matters.

signals.heading: Four current signals about making visual promises legible.

fieldNotes.title: Meta makes open science visible through concrete research projects
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta's Open Source AI for Science Summit brought researchers together to show how open-weight models are being used across scientific projects, including medicine and environmental work.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The summit gives an abstract technology a set of visible use cases. The examples do explanatory work: they let an audience see what the capability is for before asking it to believe a larger claim about the platform.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the showcased projects produce independently validated results and a repeatable path for researchers beyond the event's frame.

fieldNotes.title: Meta puts open-weight models inside concrete medical demonstrations
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta describes early-stage projects using its open-weight models for virtual-reality medical training, epilepsy research, and microscopy analysis of rare diseases.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The demonstrations give an abstract capability a visible job: train a clinician, locate a difficult signal, or reveal a pattern. The context carries more persuasive weight than the model label alone, while the company also flags that the work is investigational.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether later clinical or research results validate the demonstrations beyond the explanatory power of the examples.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI shows general models crossing into protein design
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI reports that its GPT-6 family designed protein shapes and sequences using reasoning and code, with lab tests finding binding evidence across five targets; the report also says specialized models were still used in parts of the workflow.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The visual promise is made concrete by a design brief, a lab test, and a stated limitation. That combination makes the capability easier to understand without pretending the surrounding system has disappeared.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether future work closes the gap between an impressive component capability and a reliable end-to-end biological design workflow.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI frames intelligence as a compression problem
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI's research essay explains modern AI through the idea of training a compressor or predictor on a very large corpus of data, then asks what that framing implies for intelligence and capability.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A difficult technical idea becomes more graspable when it is given a single organizing image. The frame does not prove the claim, but it gives readers a structure they can use to inspect the argument.
fieldNotes.watch: Which parts of the compression analogy continue to clarify model behavior, and where the metaphor hides important limitations.

tweets.author: Eric S. Raymond
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
Panic fatigue.

I've been thinking about why the op against Jensen Huang failed, and now I wonder if we might be seeing the end of a major phase of American politics.

Ever since the 1960s American politics has been arguably dominated by a series of panics. The population bomb. Global cooling. Global warming. AIDS. Acid rain. COVID. Peak oil. Swine flu. Mad cow disease. The coming mass famines. Saturday night specials. Satanic panic. Even, killer bees. And today, AI apocalypse. More could be added.

Over and over again the same pattern. Fear-mongering. Media hype. Most importantly, political power grabs at various scales. "Disaster is coming! Surrender your liberty so we can keep you safe!"

Skeptics stigmatized not with the language of science but with moral condemnation. Censorship deployed to silence dissenters.

And then the failure of prediction, the apocalypse that never arrives...and the panic-mongers never, ever acknowledging that they were wrong. Never being held accountable for the damage they did.

But after every cycle, the bureaucratic state is just a bit more smothering, keeping some of the reach it gained during the crisis. Everything gets more expensive. The quality of American Life degrades. Social trust weakens.

Go through this enough times, and it is not surprising that people start developing panic fatigue - reflexively looking for the con behind the hype. They start asking "Where's the power grab this time? Who benefits?"

This time, the EA/Doomer network tried to gin up a full scale panic about runaway superintelligence when it was really about making a regulatory moat for a handful of AI cloud providers, and suppressing open source AI to lock down the future. Huang was pushed out because he is a powerful voice against all that.

And people noticed. It didn't take months, or even weeks. In less than 11 days, the time it took for Huang to be reinstated, the attempt to suppress open source became an everybody knows that everybody knows thing.

And then the public case against Jensen Huang fell apart. Not the private complaint that his wife and his family legitimately has, but the rationale for his ouster.

Dare I hope that, as a society, we are becoming skeptical enough not to be fooled again? To notice when we're being played?

I think we need a name for this monster. "Witch hunt" doesn't quite cover it because that is a panic directed at marginalized individuals, rather than a power grab over the whole of society. "Moral panic" isn't quite right either, even though there is pretty much always an element of moral panic; it short-changes the political dimension.

A robot friend suggests the following...

Panic imperialism: The political exploitation of a real, exaggerated, or fabricated threat to legitimate expansions of institutional power and social control that are disproportionate to the actual requirements of addressing the threat.

The definition is good. I'm not quite satisfied with the label. The robot also suggested "apocalyptic statism" which is in some ways better.

The point is, to learn how to recognize when this playbook is being run, and jump on it before it builds a lot of momentum.

I think AI itself may have helped. It's easier than it has ever been to fact-check panic hype, and people are doing it.

Stay skeptical. Watch for the sleight of hand. We're in an information-rich, intelligence-rich environment now; they can't really fool you unless you let them.

Don't let them.
